 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                  §                OF TEXAS
                                                 §


   ROWAN DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE LLC COMMENTS ON PROPOSAL FOR
                 PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC § 25.194

        Rowan Digital Infrastructure LLC (“Rowan”), acting on its own behalf and on behalf of its
project-level subsidiaries that are developing data centers in ERCOT, welcomes the opportunity
to provide comments in response to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”)
Proposal for Publication of new 16 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) § 25.194 relating to Large
Load Interconnection Standards (the “Proposal for Publication” or “PFP”), published in Project
No. 58481 implementing Senate Bill 6 (“SB 6”) and Public Utility Regulatory Act (“PURA”) §
37.0561. Rowan is a build-to-suit sustainable data center developer that owns and operates the data
centers it builds and leases to hyperscale tenants. Rowan is committed to long-term investment in
the communities where its data centers are located, including regular investments in science,
technology, engineering, and math (“STEM”) education centers, workforce housing, and
partnerships with organizations such as Habitat for Humanity. Rowan is also committed to
building facilities that minimize data center water usage. Rowan’s Texas projects utilize a fully
closed-loop cooling system that does not require a continuous water supply.

                                     I.      INTRODUCTION
        Rowan has actively participated in the stakeholder process for Project No. 58481, including
by filing comments on the first and second discussion drafts of this rule. Rowan appreciates the
Commission’s and Staff’s responsiveness to stakeholder feedback throughout this process. As set
forth below, Rowan supports several changes reflected in the PFP that are consistent with positions
that Rowan has advocated throughout this proceeding. Rowan also identifies certain remaining
concerns regarding the PFP that Rowan respectfully requests that the Commission address in the
final rule.



                                                 1
                 II.    SUPPORT FOR CHANGES TO THE PROPOSED RULE
   Rowan supports the Commission’s changes to distinguish between the roles of the
interconnecting transmission service provider (“TSP”) and the interconnecting distribution service
provider (“DSP”) throughout the PFP. In its prior comments on the discussion draft versions of
this rule, Rowan recommended that the Commission recognize the distinct roles of these entities
in the interconnection process, as the TSP owns and operates the facilities necessary to
interconnect the large load customer to the ERCOT system, while the DSP is certificated to provide
retail electric delivery service. The PFP now includes separate definitions for “interconnecting
distribution service provider (DSP)” and “interconnecting transmission service provider (TSP)” in
subsection (c)(4) and (c)(5) and requires that three-party agreements specifically identify each
entity’s responsibilities where the DSP and TSP are different entities. This is generally consistent
with Rowan’s prior recommendations and appropriately reflects the actual roles of these entities
in the interconnection process. Rowan supports these provisions.
   Rowan also supports the PFP’s expansion of the allowable methods of demonstrating site
control in the intermediate and interconnection agreements. In its prior comments, Rowan
advocated for the inclusion of an option to purchase or lease as an acceptable method of site control
at the intermediate agreement stage and a purchase and sale agreement (“PSA”) as an acceptable
method of site control at the interconnection agreement stage, noting that these are the methods of
site control that Rowan uses at comparable stages of the interconnection process in other
jurisdictions across the country. Under subsection (d)(1)(C) of the PFP, “a signed and executed
agreement with an option to purchase or lease” one or more parcels of land sufficient to
accommodate the customer’s planned facilities at the proposed location is an acceptable method
of site control at the intermediate agreement stage. At the interconnection agreement stage, the
PFP permits “a signed and executed purchase and sales agreement,” as set forth in subsection
(f)(1)(C). These additions appropriately balance the Commission’s interest in screening
speculative projects with the practical realities of commercial real estate transactions, where
developers typically do not complete the purchase of land until they have confirmed that power
can be obtained at a site. Rowan supports these provisions.
   Rowan further supports the Commission’s decision to reduce the financial security requirement
from $100,000 per MW, as reflected in subsection (d)(10) of the PFP. In its prior comments,
Rowan, along with multiple other stakeholders, expressed concern that the $100,000 per MW

                                                 2
 financial security requirement was excessive and could unintentionally exclude financially viable
projects from the interconnection process. The reduction to $50,000 per MW moves this
requirement in the right direction and better balances the Commission’s objective of screening
speculative loads with the statutory mandate under PURA § 37.0561 to support business
development in this state. Rowan supports this change, although Rowan recommends that the
dollar-per-MW financial security be further lowered to $20,000 per MW, which would remain
sufficient to screen speculative projects and align the requirement with commercially viable large
load development.

                                III.    ADDITIONAL CONCERNS
   Notwithstanding the improvements described above, Rowan respectfully identifies the
following remaining concerns with the PFP.

   A. Site Control Requirements of Intermediate Agreement Stage
   First, Rowan notes a potential drafting issue in the site control provisions at the intermediate
agreement stage. Subsection (d)(1)(A) of the PFP requires a lease to have “a duration of at least
five years from the date the large load customer is expected to reach the contracted peak demand.”
However, “contracted peak demand” is defined in subsection (c)(3) as the demand stated in the
interconnection agreement. At the intermediate agreement stage, the interconnection agreement
has not yet been executed, and therefore no “contracted peak demand” has been established.
Rowan believes Staff may have intended to use the term “requested peak demand” in subsection
(d)(1)(A), as “requested peak demand” is defined in subsection (c)(10) as the demand prior to
executing an interconnection agreement. Rowan recommends that the Commission revise
subsection (d)(1)(A) to reference “requested peak demand” rather than “contracted peak demand.”

   B. Refundability of Financial Requirements
   Rowan has significant concerns regarding the refundability provisions of the PFP. While
Rowan supports the Commission’s objective of deterring speculative interconnection requests, the
requirement to pay non-refundable study fees and post substantial financial security is, in itself, a
meaningful deterrent. The PFP’s refundability provisions, especially the 80/20 forfeiture upon
withdrawal under subsections (g)(3)-(4) and (h)(3)-(4), the non-refundable interconnection fee
under subsection (f)(7), and the five-year sustained operations requirement for full refund under


                                                 3
 subsection (i), go well beyond what is necessary to screen speculative projects and impose
disproportionate financial penalties on legitimate large load customers. As discussed in detail
below, Rowan respectfully recommends that the Commission revise the PFP’s refundability
provisions at both the intermediate agreement and interconnection agreement stages to ensure that
the financial consequences of withdrawal or delayed energization are proportionate to the costs
actually incurred and consistent with the Texas Legislature’s intent to facilitate large load
interconnection under PURA § 37.0561.

       1. Intermediate Agreement Stage
               a. 80/20 Forfeiture Structure Upon Withdrawal

       Rowan is concerned about the treatment of financial security posted on a dollar-per-MW
basis under subsection (d)(10) and financial security for significant equipment or services under
subsection (d)(11) upon a large load customer’s withdrawal of requested peak demand.
Subsections (g)(3) and (g)(4) of the PFP provide that, upon a large load customer’s withdrawal of
all or a portion of its requested peak demand, after applying financial security to outstanding
amounts owed, only 20% of the remaining balance is refunded to the large load customer, while
the remaining 80% is paid to the interconnecting TSP as an offset to the TSP’s rate base.
       The PFP does not provide a justification for permitting the interconnecting TSP to retain
80% of a large load customer’s financial security upon withdrawal. The requirement to post
substantial financial security paid on a dollar-per-MW basis, which can amount to tens of millions
of dollars for a data center project, already serves as a meaningful deterrent against speculative
interconnection requests. A large load customer that is willing and able to post financial security
of this scale has demonstrated a serious commitment to the interconnection process, and the
opportunity cost of tying up significant capital for the duration of the process provides a strong
incentive against frivolous or speculative requests. Imposing an additional penalty by limiting
refunds to 20% of the remaining balance upon withdrawal is therefore unnecessary to achieve the
Commission’s screening objective.
       Further, retaining 80% of the remaining financial security, particularly when combined
with the non-refundable study fee under subsection (d)(9), results in an undue and disproportionate
financial penalty on large load customers that may withdraw for legitimate commercial reasons,
including due to circumstances beyond their control. This outcome is not appropriately tied to

                                                4
 costs actually incurred by the interconnecting DSP or TSP. Excessive punitive forfeiture
provisions also risk discouraging phased development, resizing, or early disclosure of changing
project assumptions, which are behaviors that support accurate transmission planning. Deterrence
should be achieved through meaningful financial commitment, not through forfeiture structures
that discourage transparency and adaptive project execution.
       Accordingly, Rowan respectfully submits that the Commission should revise the PFP to
provide for a full refund of both the financial security on a dollar-per-MW basis under subsection
(d)(10) and the financial security for significant equipment and services under subsection (d)(11),
less any outstanding amounts owed for costs actually incurred by the interconnecting DSP or
interconnecting TSP under subsection (g), when a customer withdraws an interconnection request
at the intermediate agreement stage. Under this revision, a large load customer would receive a
refund of its remaining financial security, regardless of whether withdrawal occurs before or after
an interconnection study. Where no study has been performed, the interconnecting DSP and TSP
will have incurred minimal costs, and retention of financial security is not justified. Where a study
has been performed but no interconnection agreement has been executed, the customer has already
paid the non-refundable study fee, and any remaining financial security, after reduction for actual
costs incurred, should be refunded.
       Alternatively, if the Commission determines that some portion of financial security should
remain non-refundable, Rowan urges the Commission to increase the refundable percentage well
above 20%. Allowing the TSP to retain 80% of the financial security is excessive and not
sufficiently tied to the objective of deterring speculative load requests. Rowan proposes that the
Commission revise subsections (g)(3) and (g)(4) to provide that no less than 80% of the remaining
financial security balance, after application to outstanding amounts owed for costs actually
incurred, be refunded to the large load customer upon withdrawal, with the interconnecting TSP
retaining no more than 20% as a rate base offset. This revised allocation would still impose a
meaningful financial consequence for withdrawal, while ensuring that the penalty is proportionate
to the Commission’s stated objective of deterring speculative interconnection requests. To the
extent the Commission determines that a different allocation is appropriate, Rowan respectfully
requests that the Commission clearly articulate a rationale tied to the policy objectives of PURA §
37.0561 and the costs that the interconnecting TSP is reasonably expected to incur.



                                                 5
                  b. Refund for Post-Study Service Reduction
        In addition to its recommendations regarding full withdrawal of an interconnection request,
Rowan also recommends that the PFP address the treatment of financial security where an
interconnection study determines that the interconnecting TSP cannot serve the large load
customer’s full requested peak demand or cannot serve the full requested peak demand or cannot
serve the requested peak demand on the commercially reasonable energization timeline identified
by the customer, including circumstances where the full MWs can be served only on a materially
delayed schedule.
        In circumstances where the TSP cannot serve the full requested peak demand, the large
load customer’s financial security obligations should be reduced to correspond to the peak demand
that the system can actually serve. 1 Specifically, the large load customer should receive a refund
of the dollar-per-MW financial security corresponding to the MWs of requested peak demand that
cannot be served. Additionally, if the reduced MW allocation results in reduced costs for
significant equipment and services, the large load customer should receive a corresponding refund
of the financial security posted for such equipment and services, unless such financial security can
be applied to other obligations under the interconnection agreement. Requiring a large load
customer to forfeit financial security for capacity that the transmission system cannot deliver is
inconsistent with the fundamental ratemaking principle that customers should bear only the costs
they cause. When system‑driven constraints result in punitive financial penalties, customers are
discouraged from early transparency and adaptive resizing, creating incentives for over‑reservation
or delayed disclosure that increase transmission planning risk. Allowing refunds that reflect
post‑study conditions better supports accurate load forecasting and efficient system planning.

        2. Interconnection Agreement Stage
                 a. Interconnection Fee
    Rowan has significant concerns regarding the non-refundability of the interconnection fee at
the interconnection agreement stage. Subsection (f)(7) of the PFP requires a large load customer
to pay a non-refundable interconnection fee in the amount of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak
demand. For a large-scale data center project, this non-refundable fee could amount to tens of


1
 This partial refund should also be available if the customer’s full requested peak demand cannot be served on a
commercially reasonable timeline and the customer opts to proceed with interconnection of only a portion of its
previously requested peak demand.

                                                         6
 millions of dollars. While Rowan understands the Commission’s interest in ensuring that large
load customers demonstrate financial commitment, a wholly non-refundable fee of this magnitude
raises concerns about the proportionality of the financial burden imposed on large load customers.
Rowan’s recommendations are grounded in the longstanding Texas ratemaking principle that
customers should bear only those costs they cause and that utilities should recover only those costs
related to interconnection of load actually incurred.
   Rowan recommends that the Commission consider making the interconnection fee refundable,
in whole or in part, upon energization or upon the large load customer’s achievement of milestones
in its schedule for phased energization. At a minimum, the interconnection fee should be
refundable to the extent that it exceeds the interconnecting TSP’s actual costs incurred in
connection with the interconnection.
   Additionally, Rowan notes that subsection (f)(7) does not expressly state the acceptable forms
of payment for the interconnection fee. Unlike other provisions of the PFP addressing financial
security—which expressly permit cash collateral, corporate or parental guaranty, or letter of
credit—subsection (f)(7) is silent on payment options. While subsection (f)(7)(A) requires the
interconnecting DSP or interconnecting TSP to draw down on any unused financial security posted
under the intermediate agreement to satisfy the interconnection fee, which implies that any of the
financial security forms accepted under the intermediate agreement could apply, this is not
expressly stated. Rowan recommends that the Commission clarify the acceptable forms of payment
for the interconnection fee to provide certainty to large load customers and interconnecting
utilities. The rule should expressly provide that the interconnection fee may be satisfied through
the same forms of financial security permitted elsewhere in the PFP, including cash collateral,
corporate or parental guaranty, and letters of credit.

               b. Potential Drafting Issue in (f)(8)(B)
   Rowan also identifies a potential drafting issue in subsection (f)(8)(B) of the PFP. That
subsection provides that, “[a]fter drawing down on financial security posted under an intermediate
agreement for payment of the interconnection fee,” the interconnecting DSP or interconnecting
TSP must apply the balance of any unused financial security to satisfy the financial security for
significant equipment or services. However, the interconnection fee is not paid under the
intermediate agreement—it is an obligation arising under the interconnection agreement pursuant


                                                  7
 to subsection (f)(7). Rowan recommends that the Commission revise subsection (f)(8)(B) to
accurately reflect the sequencing of financial obligations under the PFP.

               c. Refund after Energization
   Additionally, subsection (i)(1)-(2) of the PFP provides that even for a large load customer that
energizes, only 20% of the remaining financial security balance is refunded when the customer
energizes (and ratably as the customer meets milestones in its schedule for phased energization),
with the remaining balance refunded only after the customer sustains operations for five years at
contracted peak demand. The five-year sustained operations requirement imposes an extended
period of financial uncertainty on large load customers that have already demonstrated their
commitment by energizing and meeting milestones. Rowan recommends that the Commission
revise subsection (i) to provide for more timely refunds upon energization and milestone
achievement, rather than requiring a large load customer to sustain operations for five years before
receiving a full refund.
   Rowan recommends that the Commission adopt the following refund schedule for each
category of financial security after that financial security has been applied to outstanding amounts
owed: (i) 60% of the remaining balance refunded upon initial energization; (ii) 20% of the
remaining balance refunded upon the large load customer achieving 50% of its contracted peak
demand; and (iii) the final 20% of the remaining balance refunded upon the large load customer
achieving 100% of its contracted peak demand. A refund schedule tied to objective, verifiable
energization milestones appropriately balances the Commission’s interest in ensuring that large
load customers follow through on their interconnection commitments with the need to avoid
imposing prolonged financial uncertainty on customers that have demonstrated their commitment
through actual energization and load growth.
   Rowan further notes that subsection (i) applies only to financial security for significant
equipment or services and financial security for system upgrades; it does not apply to the initial
$50,000 per MW financial security posted under subsection (d)(10) at the intermediate agreement
stage. As a result, the dollar-per-MW financial security is not subject to any refund upon
energization, even where the large load customer has fully energized and is operating at its
contracted peak demand. Rowan recommends that the Commission revise the PFP to provide that
the dollar-per-MW financial security posted under subsection (d)(10) is also refundable upon
energization, less any outstanding amounts owed for costs actually incurred. The continued
                                                 8
 non-refundability of the dollar-per-MW financial security after full energization and sustained
operation is particularly concerning. Once a large load customer has energized and is operating at
its contracted peak demand, there is no remaining speculative or stranded-cost risk to justify
retention of this security.
    To the extent the Commission determines that some portion of financial security should be
retained upon withdrawal to deter speculative projects, Rowan recommends that the retained
percentage be significantly reduced from 80% and that the Commission provide a clear rationale
for any retained amount that is tied to the policy objectives of PURA § 37.0561.

                d. 80/20 Forfeiture Structure Upon Withdrawal
        Rowan also has significant concerns regarding the treatment of financial security upon
withdrawal at the interconnection agreement stage. For the same reasons set forth above regarding
the intermediate agreement stage, Rowan recommends that the Commission revise subsections
(g)(3) and (g)(4) to provide for a full refund of financial security (less any outstanding amounts
owed to the interconnecting DSP or TSP for actual costs incurred) upon withdrawal, rather than
retaining 80% of the balance as a rate base offset. The 80/20 forfeiture structure imposes a
disproportionate financial penalty on large load customers, particularly where the interconnecting
TSP has not incurred costs commensurate with the retained financial security.

              e. True Up Between Intermediate Agreement and Interconnection
                  Agreement Financial Security Requirements
    Rowan further recommends that the PFP be revised to require a true-up process to ensure that
financial security posted under the intermediate agreement is properly credited toward the financial
security and interconnection fee obligations arising under the interconnection agreement. Absent
such a mechanism, a large load customer could be required to post duplicative financial security,
resulting in an excessive and unwarranted financial burden.
    Rowan also recommends that the PFP include a refund process for circumstances in which the
financial security posted under the intermediate agreement exceeds the financial security and
interconnection fee obligations required under the interconnection agreement. To the extent that a
large load customer’s financial obligations are reduced upon execution of the interconnection
agreement, the large load customer should be entitled to a prompt refund of the excess financial
security. For example, excess financial security should be refunded if a customer’s contracted peak
demand under the interconnection agreement is lower than the customer’s requested peak demand

                                                 9
 because the interconnection study indicates that only a portion of the customer’s requested peak
demand can be served.

   C. Third Party Payment
   Third, Rowan recommends that the PFP expressly permit a large load customer’s tenant,
prospective tenant, or other third party to post financial security directly to the interconnecting
TSP or interconnecting DSP on behalf of the large load customer, provided that the third party in
question (i) meets commercially reasonable creditworthiness standards and (ii) is expressly
obligated to post such security under a written contract with the large load customer. The PFP
currently permits the use of a corporate or parental guaranty as an acceptable form of financial
security under subsections (d)(10)(C)(ii) and (f)(8)(C)(ii). However, in Rowan’s experience
developing data center projects across the country, it is common for a hyperscale tenant to provide
a parent company guaranty to satisfy financial security requirements on behalf of the build-to-suit
developer. Expressly permitting this arrangement in the rule would reduce the financial burden on
build-to-suit developers, while still ensuring that the interconnecting TSP or DSP receives
adequate financial security. This approach is consistent with the Commission’s objective of
supporting business development in Texas, as it enables a broader range of developers, not just the
largest hyperscale companies, to participate in the interconnection process.
   Rowan appreciates the Commission’s consideration of these comments and looks forward to
continued engagement in this proceeding. Rowan respectfully requests that the Commission
address the concerns identified herein in the final rule.


Dated April 17, 2026


Respectfully submitted,


Tyler Petersen
Director of Regulatory Affairs and Public Policy
tpetersen@rowan.digital
ROWAN DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE LLC

                     Proposed Revisions to the Proposal for Publication:


§25.194. Large Load Interconnection Standards.
(a)   Purpose and Scope. This section sets forth the standards and criteria for an electric utility,
      a municipally owned utility, and electric cooperative to interconnect a large load customer
      to the ERCOT system. Nothing in this section limits the authority of a municipally owned
      utility or an electric cooperative to impose electric service requirements for large load
      customers on their systems in addition to the standards adopted under this section.


(b)   Applicability. This section applies to a large load customer that seeks:
      (1)    a new interconnection that is equal to or exceeds 75 megawatts (MW);
      (2)    an expanded interconnection that equals or exceeds 75 MW for the first time; and
      (3)    an expanded interconnection that exceeds 75 MW by 75 MW or more.


(c)   Definitions. The following words and terms, when used in this section, have the following
      meanings unless the context indicates otherwise:
      (1)    Backup generating facilities -- Generation facilities or energy storage facilities
             that are not capable of operating, or are not configured to operate, in parallel with
             the ERCOT system and cannot export energy to the ERCOT system.
      (2)    Competitively sensitive information -- Competitively sensitive information
             includes exact site locations, such as parcel identifiers or property boundaries;
             commercial terms, such as pricing or internal development prioritization;
             proprietary architectural, operational, or compute-deployment strategies; and
             financing structures. Competitively sensitive information does not include the
             identity of a large load customer; general site location, such as load zone; requested
             or contracted peak demand; timing of energization; or whether an interconnection
             request is associated with the same applicant or affiliated entities.
      (3)    Contracted peak demand -- The total non-coincident peak demand that a large
             load customer requests that an interconnecting DSP or an interconnecting TSP
             serve at a site as stated interconnection agreement.



                                               11
       (4)    Interconnecting distribution service provider (DSP) -- The electric utility,
             municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that is certificated to provide
             retail electric delivery service at the location in which the large load customer seeks
             to interconnect.
      (5)    Interconnecting transmission service provider (TSP) -- The electric utility,
             municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that owns and operates the
             facilities necessary to interconnect the large load customer to the ERCOT system.
      (6)    Interconnection agreement -- An agreement that is executed by a large load
             customer, the interconnecting DSP, and, if different from the interconnecting DSP,
             the interconnecting TSP after completion of the interconnection study and that, at
             a minimum, satisfies subsection (f) of this section.
      (7)    Interconnection study -- The set of studies that are required by ERCOT before a
             large load customer may be interconnected.
      (8)    Intermediate agreement -- An agreement that is executed by a large load
             customer, the interconnecting DSP, and, if different from the interconnecting DSP,
             the interconnecting TSP before the interconnection study are initiated and that, at a
             minimum, satisfies subsection (d) of this section.
      (9)    Large load customer -- An entity requesting a new or expanded interconnection
             where the customer’s total expected non-coincident peak demand at a single site is
             equal to or exceeds 75 MW.
      (10)   Requested peak demand -- The total non-coincident peak demand that a large load
             customer requests, prior to executing an interconnection agreement, that an
             interconnecting DSP or an interconnecting TSP serve at a site.


(d)   Intermediate agreement. Before a large load interconnection request is submitted to
      ERCOT for study, the large load customer must execute an intermediate agreement with
      the interconnecting DSP and, if different from the interconnecting DSP, the interconnecting
      TSP. If the interconnecting DSP and the interconnecting TSP are different entities, the
      intermediate agreement must specifically identify each entity’s responsibilities under this
      section, including which entity will accept the study fee and financial security from the



                                               12
 large load customer. The intermediate agreement must meet the requirements of this
subsection.
(1)    Site control. A large load customer must demonstrate site control for the proposed
       load location through provision of one of the following property interests to the
       interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP:
       (A)    a signed and executed lease agreement for one or more parcels of land
              sufficient to accommodate the customer’s planned facilities at the proposed
              load location for a duration of at least five years from the date the large load
              customer is expected to reach the requested contracted peak demand;
       (B)    a deed for one or more parcels of land sufficient to accommodate the
              customer’s planned facilities at the proposed load location; or
       (C)    a signed and executed agreement with an option to purchase or lease one or
              more parcels of land sufficient to accommodate the customer’s planned
              facilities at the proposed location.
(2)    Substantially similar interconnection request. A large load customer must
       disclose to the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP whether the
       customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request for electric
       service, the approval of which would result in the customer materially changing,
       delaying, or withdrawing the interconnection request. A material change or delay
       includes a delay of one or more years to the project’s projected date to realize its
       requested or contracted peak demand, a 20% or greater change in the requested or
       contracted peak demand, or a change in the location for the point of interconnection.
       (A)    A large load customer that is pursuing a substantially similar
              interconnection request for electric service the approval of which would
              result in the customer materially changing, delaying, or withdrawing the
              interconnection request must disclose the following information to the
              interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP:
              (i)     the ERCOT-assigned serial number (i.e., the large load
                      interconnection     number)      for    the    substantially    similar
                      interconnection request, as applicable;



                                        13
              (ii)    the location, including the power region and, if in the ERCOT
                     region, the load zone, of the substantially similar interconnection
                     request;
             (iii)   the non-coincident peak demand of the substantially similar
                     interconnection request;
             (iv)    the anticipated timing of energization of the substantially similar
                     interconnection request; and
             (v)     the interconnecting DSP and, if different from the interconnecting
                     DSP, the interconnecting TSP associated with the substantially
                     similar interconnection request.
      (B)    A large load customer that discloses a substantially similar interconnection
             request under this subsection may anonymize competitively sensitive
             information in its disclosure to the interconnecting DSP or the
             interconnecting TSP.
      (C)    An interconnecting DSP and an interconnecting TSP must not sell, share,
             or disclose information submitted to the interconnecting DSP or the
             interconnecting TSP under this subsection other than a disclosure to the
             commission or ERCOT.
      (D)    ERCOT may request and the large load customer must provide any
             competitively sensitive information ERCOT deems necessary to complete
             any analysis required as part of the interconnection process. ERCOT must
             treat disclosed competitively sensitive information as Protected Information
             under ERCOT protocols.
(3)   Site-related studies and engineering services. A large load customer must submit
      to the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP the large load customer’s
      plans, expected timing, and progress for site-related studies and engineering
      services required for project development before energization (e.g., geotechnical
      survey, water, wastewater, or gas). The submission must be accompanied by an
      attestation by an officer or official with binding authority over the large load
      customer stating that the information contained in the submission is complete and
      accurate at the time the attestation is signed. A large load customer must provide

                                      14
       updates or progress reports to the interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP
      when requested, but no more frequently than quarterly.
(4)   State and local regulatory approvals. A large load customer must submit to the
      interconnecting DSP or the interconnecting TSP the large load customer’s plans,
      expected timing, and current progress for obtaining non-ministerial discretionary
      approvals from state and local regulatory authorities required for development
      before energization (e.g., water, air, or backup generation permits). The submission
      must be accompanied by an attestation by an officer or official with binding
      authority over the large load customer attesting that the information contained in
      the submission is complete and accurate at the time the attestation is signed. A

                                    EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

•   Rowan supports the PFP’s distinction between the interconnecting TSP and interconnecting DSP,
    including separate definitions and the requirement that agreements identify each entity’s
    responsibilities, which is generally consistent with Rowan’s prior recommendations.
•   Rowan supports the PFP’s expansion of allowable site control methods to include an option to
    purchase or lease at the intermediate agreement stage and a PSA at the interconnection agreement
    stage, which is consistent with Rowan’s prior advocacy for options and PSAs as acceptable forms
    of site control at these stages.
•   Rowan supports the reduction of the financial security requirement from $100,000 per MW, which
    better balances the need to screen speculative loads without unduly hindering large load
    development in Texas. While the reduction to $50,000 per MW moves the rule in the right direction,
    Rowan would recommend a further reduction to $20,000 per MW.
•   Rowan identifies a potential drafting issue in subsection (d)(1)(A), which references “contracted
    peak demand” in the context of the intermediate agreement; Rowan recommends this be revised to
    “requested peak demand,” as the interconnection agreement establishing contracted peak demand
    has not yet been executed at the intermediate agreement stage.
•   Rowan has significant concerns regarding the refundability provisions at both the intermediate
    agreement and interconnection agreement stages, including the 80/20 forfeiture upon withdrawal
    under subsections (g)(3)-(4), the non-refundable interconnection fee under subsection (f)(7), and
    the five-year sustained operations requirement under subsection (i), and recommends that financial
    security be fully refundable (less actual costs incurred) upon withdrawal or energization.
•   Rowan recommends that the Commission adopt a milestone-based refund schedule for refunds
    related to energization, which would provide for 60% refund upon initial energization, 20% upon
    achieving half of contracted peak demand, and the final 20% upon achieving full contracted peak

                 II.     SUPPORT FOR CHANGES TO THE PROPOSED RULE
   Rowan supports the Commission' s changes to distinguish between the roles of the
interconnecting transmission service provider ("TSP") and the interconnecting distribution service
provider ("DSP") throughout the PFP. In its prior comments on the discussion draft versions of
this rule, Rowan recommended that the Commission recognize the distinct roles of these entities
in the interconnection process, as the TSP owns and operates the facilities necessary to
interconnect the large load customer to the ERCOT system, while the DSP is certificated to provide
retail electric delivery service. The PFP now includes separate definitions for "interconnecting
distribution service provider (DSP)" and "interconnecting transmission service provider (TSP)" in
subsection (c)(4) and (c)(5) and requires that three-party agreements specifically identify each
entity' s responsibilities where the DSP and TSP are different entities. This is generally consistent

   Rowan also supports the PFP's expansion of the allowable methods of demonstrating site
control in the intermediate and interconnection agreements. In its prior comments, Rowan
advocated for the inclusion of an option to purchase or lease as an acceptable method of site control

method of site control at the interconnection agreement stage, noting that these are the methods of

agreement with an option to purchase or lease" one or more parcels of land sufficient to
accommodate the customer's planned facilities at the proposed location is an acceptable method
of site control at the intermediate agreement stage. At the interconnection agreement stage, the
PFP permits "a signed and executed purchase and sales agreement," as set forth in subsection

speculative proj ects with the practical realities of commercial real estate transactions, where
developers typically do not complete the purchase of land until they have confirmed that power
can be obtained at a site. Rowan supports these provisions.
   Rowan further supports the Commission' s decision to reduce the financial security requirement
from $100,000 per MW, as reflected in subsection (d)(10) of the PFP. In its prior comments,
Rowan, along with multiple other stakeholders, expressed concern that the $100,000 per MW

 financial security requirement was excessive and could unintentionally exclude financially viable
projects from the interconnection process. The reduction to $50,000 per MW moves this
requirement in the right direction and better balances the Commission' s objective of screening
speculative loads with the statutory mandate under PURA § 37.0561 to support business
development in this state. Rowan supports this change, although Rowan recommends that the
dollar-per-MW financial security be further lowered to $20,000 per MW, which would remain
sufficient to screen speculative proj ects and align the requirement with commercially viable large

                                III.    ADDITIONAL CONCERNS
   Notwithstanding the improvements described above, Rowan respectfully identifies the
following remaining concerns with the PFP.

   A. Site Control Requirements of Intermediate Agreement Stage
   First, Rowan notes a potential drafting issue in the site control provisions at the intermediate
agreement stage. Subsection (d)(1)(A) of the PFP requires a lease to have "a duration of at least
five years from the date the large load customer is expected to reach the contracted peak demand."
However, "contracted peak demand" is defined in subsection (c)(3) as the demand stated in the
interconnection agreement. At the intermediate agreement stage, the interconnection agreement
has not yet been executed, and therefore no "contracted peak demand" has been established.
Rowan believes Staff may have intended to use the term "requested peak demand" in subsection
(d)(1)(A), as "requested peak demand" is defined in subsection (c)(10) as the demand prior to
executing an interconnection agreement. Rowan recommends that the Commission revise
subsection (d)(1)(A) to reference "requested peak demand" rather than "contracted peak demand."

   B. Refundability of Financial Requirements
   Rowan has significant concerns regarding the refundability provisions of the PFP. While
Rowan supports the Commission' s obj ective of deterring speculative interconnection requests, the
requirement to pay non-refundable study fees and post substantial financial security is, in itself, a
meaningful deterrent. The PFP' s refundability provisions, especially the 80/20 forfeiture upon
withdrawal under subsections (g)(3)-(4) and (h)(3)-(4), the non-refundable interconnection fee
under subsection (f)(7), and the five-year sustained operations requirement for full refund under


                                                 3
 subsection (i), go well beyond what is necessary to screen speculative projects and impose
disproportionate financial penalties on legitimate large load customers. As discussed in detail
below, Rowan respectfully recommends that the Commission revise the PFP' s refundability
provisions at both the intermediate agreement and interconnection agreement stages to ensure that
the financial consequences of withdrawal or delayed energization are proportionate to the costs
actually incurred and consistent with the Texas Legislature' s intent to facilitate large load
interconnection under PURA § 37.0561.

       1. Intermediate Agreement Stage
               a. 80/20 Forfeiture Structure Upon Withdrawal

       Rowan is concerned about the treatment of financial security posted on a dollar-per-MW
basis under subsection (d)(10) and financial security for significant equipment or services under
subsection (d)(11) upon a large load customer' s withdrawal of requested peak demand.
Subsections (g)(3) and (g)(4) of the PFP provide that, upon a large load customer' s withdrawal of
all or a portion of its requested peak demand, after applying financial security to outstanding
amounts owed, only 20% of the remaining balance is refunded to the large load customer, while
the remaining 80% is paid to the interconnecting TSP as an offset to the TSP' s rate base.
       The PFP does not provide a justification for permitting the interconnecting TSP to retain
80% of a large load customer' s financial security upon withdrawal. The requirement to post
substantial financial security paid on a dollar-per-MW basis, which can amount to tens of millions
of dollars for a data center proj ect, already serves as a meaningful deterrent against speculative
interconnection requests. A large load customer that is willing and able to post financial security
of this scale has demonstrated a serious commitment to the interconnection process, and the
opportunity cost of tying up significant capital for the duration of the process provides a strong
incentive against frivolous or speculative requests. Imposing an additional penalty by limiting
refunds to 20% of the remaining balance upon withdrawal is therefore unnecessary to achieve the
Commission' s screening objective.
       Further, retaining 80% of the remaining financial security, particularly when combined
with the non-refundable study fee under subsection (d)(9), results in an undue and disproportionate
financial penalty on large load customers that may withdraw for legitimate commercial reasons,
including due to circumstances beyond their control. This outcome is not appropriately tied to

                                                4
 costs actually incurred by the interconnecting DSP or TSP. Excessive punitive forfeiture
provisions also risk discouraging phased development, resizing, or early disclosure of changing
proj ect assumptions, which are behaviors that support accurate transmission planning. Deterrence
should be achieved through meaningful financial commitment, not through forfeiture structures
that discourage transparency and adaptive proj ect execution.
       Accordingly, Rowan respectfully submits that the Commission should revise the PFP to
provide for a full refund of both the financial security on a dollar-per-MW basis under subsection
(d)(10) and the financial security for significant equipment and services under subsection (d)(11),
less any outstanding amounts owed for costs actually incurred by the interconnecting DSP or
interconnecting TSP under subsection (g), when a customer withdraws an interconnection request
at the intermediate agreement stage. Under this revision, a large load customer would receive a
refund of its remaining financial security, regardless of whether withdrawal occurs before or after
an interconnection study. Where no study has been performed, the interconnecting DSP and TSP
will have incurred minimal costs, and retention of financial security is notjustified. Where a study
has been performed but no interconnection agreement has been executed, the customer has already
paid the non-refundable study fee, and any remaining financial security, after reduction for actual
costs incurred, should be refunded.
       Alternatively, ifthe Commission determines that some portion of financial security should
remain non-refundable, Rowan urges the Commission to increase the refundable percentage well
above 20%. Allowing the TSP to retain 80% of the financial security is excessive and not
sufficiently tied to the obj ective of deterring speculative load requests. Rowan proposes that the
Commission revise subsections (g)(3) and (g)(4) to provide that no less than 80% ofthe remaining
financial security balance, after application to outstanding amounts owed for costs actually
incurred, be refunded to the large load customer upon withdrawal, with the interconnecting TSP
retaining no more than 20% as a rate base offset. This revised allocation would still impose a
meaningful financial consequence for withdrawal, while ensuring that the penalty is proportionate
to the Commission' s stated obj ective of deterring speculative interconnection requests. To the
extent the Commission determines that a different allocation is appropriate, Rowan respectfully
requests that the Commission clearly articulate a rationale tied to the policy objectives of PURA §
37.0561 and the costs that the interconnecting TSP is reasonably expected to incur.

                   b. Refund for Post-Study Service Reduction
         In addition to its recommendations regarding full withdrawal of an interconnection request,
Rowan also recommends that the PFP address the treatment of financial security where an
interconnection study determines that the interconnecting TSP cannot serve the large load
customer' s full requested peak demand or cannot serve the full requested peak demand or cannot
serve the requested peak demand on the commercially reasonable energization timeline identified
by the customer, including circumstances where the full MWs can be served only on a materially
delayed schedule.
         In circumstances where the TSP cannot serve the full requested peak demand, the large
load customer' s financial security obligations should be reduced to correspond to the peak demand
that the system can actually serve. 1 Specifically, the large load customer should receive a refund
ofthe dollar-per-MW financial security corresponding to the MWs of requested peak demand that
cannot be served. Additionally, if the reduced MW allocation results in reduced costs for
significant equipment and services, the large load customer should receive a corresponding refund
ofthe financial security posted for such equipment and services, unless such financial security can
be applied to other obligations under the interconnection agreement. Requiring a large load
customer to forfeit financial security for capacity that the transmission system cannot deliver is
inconsistent with the fundamental ratemaking principle that customers should bear only the costs
they cause. When system-driven constraints result in punitive financial penalties, customers are
discouraged from early transparency and adaptive resizing, creating incentives for over-reservation
or delayed disclosure that increase transmission planning risk. Allowing refunds that reflect
post-study conditions better supports accurate load forecasting and efficient system planning.

the interconnection agreement stage. Subsection (f)(7) of the PFP requires a large load customer
to pay a non-refundable interconnection fee in the amount of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak
demand. For a large-scale data center project, this non-refundable fee could amount to tens of

 millions of dollars. While Rowan understands the Commission's interest in ensuring that large

               c. Refund after Energization
   Additionally, subsection (i)(1)-(2) of the PFP provides that even for a large load customer that
energizes, only 20% of the remaining financial security balance is refunded when the customer
energizes (and ratably as the customer meets milestones in its schedule for phased energization),
with the remaining balance refunded only after the customer sustains operations for five years at
contracted peak demand. The five-year sustained operations requirement imposes an extended
period of financial uncertainty on large load customers that have already demonstrated their
commitment by energizing and meeting milestones. Rowan recommends that the Commission
revise subsection (i) to provide for more timely refunds upon energization and milestone
achievement, rather than requiring a large load customer to sustain operations for five years before
receiving a full refund.
   Rowan recommends that the Commission adopt the following refund schedule for each
category of financial security after that financial security has been applied to outstanding amounts
owed: (i) 60% of the remaining balance refunded upon initial energization; (ii) 20% of the
remaining balance refunded upon the large load customer achieving 50% of its contracted peak
demand; and (iii) the final 20% of the remaining balance refunded upon the large load customer
achieving 100% of its contracted peak demand. A refund schedule tied to objective, verifiable
energization milestones appropriately balances the Commission's interest in ensuring that large
load customers follow through on their interconnection commitments with the need to avoid
imposing prolonged financial uncertainty on customers that have demonstrated their commitment
through actual energization and load growth.
   Rowan further notes that subsection (i) applies only to financial security for significant
equipment or services and financial security for system upgrades; it does not apply to the initial
$50,000 per MW financial security posted under subsection (d)(10) at the intermediate agreement
stage. As a result, the dollar-per-MW financial security is not subject to any refund upon
energization, even where the large load customer has fully energized and is operating at its
contracted peak demand. Rowan recommends that the Commission revise the PFP to provide that
the dollar-per-MW financial security posted under subsection (d)(10) is also refundable upon
energization, less any outstanding amounts owed for costs actually incurred. The continued

                                                 8
 non-refundability of the dollar-per-MW financial security after full energization and sustained
operation is particularly concerning. Once a large load customer has energized and is operating at
its contracted peak demand, there is no remaining speculative or stranded-cost risk to justify
retention of this security.
    To the extent the Commission determines that some portion of financial security should be
retained upon withdrawal to deter speculative proj ects, Rowan recommends that the retained
percentage be significantly reduced from 80% and that the Commission provide a clear rationale
for any retained amount that is tied to the policy objectives of PURA § 37.0561.

                d. 80/20 Forfeiture Structure Upon Withdrawal
        Rowan also has significant concerns regarding the treatment of financial security upon
withdrawal at the interconnection agreement stage. For the same reasons set forth above regarding
the intermediate agreement stage, Rowan recommends that the Commission revise subsections
(g)(3) and (g)(4) to provide for a full refund of financial security (less any outstanding amounts
owed to the interconnecting DSP or TSP for actual costs incurred) upon withdrawal, rather than
retaining 80% of the balance as a rate base offset. The 80/20 forfeiture structure imposes a
disproportionate financial penalty on large load customers, particularly where the interconnecting
TSP has not incurred costs commensurate with the retained financial security.

              e. True Up Between Intermediate Agreement and Interconnection
                  Agreement Financial Security Requirements
    Rowan further recommends that the PFP be revised to require a true-up process to ensure that
financial security posted under the intermediate agreement is properly credited toward the financial
security and interconnection fee obligations arising under the interconnection agreement. Absent
such a mechanism, a large load customer could be required to post duplicative financial security,
resulting in an excessive and unwarranted financial burden.
    Rowan also recommends that the PFP include a refund process for circumstances in which the
financial security posted under the intermediate agreement exceeds the financial security and
interconnection fee obligations required under the interconnection agreement. To the extent that a
large load customer' s financial obligations are reduced upon execution of the interconnection
agreement, the large load customer should be entitled to a prompt refund of the excess financial
security. For example, excess financial security should be refunded if a customer' s contracted peak
demand under the interconnection agreement is lower than the customer' s requested peak demand

                                                 9
 because the interconnection study indicates that only a portion of the customer' s requested peak
demand can be served.

   C. Third Party Payment
   Third, Rowan recommends that the PFP expressly permit a large load customer' s tenant,
prospective tenant, or other third party to post financial security directly to the interconnecting
TSP or interconnecting DSP on behalf of the large load customer, provided that the third party in
question (i) meets commercially reasonable creditworthiness standards and (ii) is expressly
obligated to post such security under a written contract with the large load customer. The PFP
currently permits the use of a corporate or parental guaranty as an acceptable form of financial
security under subsections (d)(10)(C)(ii) and (f)(8)(C)(ii). However, in Rowan's experience
developing data center proj ects across the country, it is common for a hyperscale tenant to provide
a parent company guaranty to satisfy financial security requirements on behalf of the build-to-suit
developer. Expressly permitting this arrangement in the rule would reduce the financial burden on
build-to-suit developers, while still ensuring that the interconnecting TSP or DSP receives
adequate financial security. This approach is consistent with the Commission's objective of
supporting business development in Texas, as it enables a broader range of developers, not just the
largest hyperscale companies, to participate in the interconnection process.
   Rowan appreciates the Commission's consideration of these comments and looks forward to
continued engagement in this proceeding. Rowan respectfully requests that the Commission
address the concerns identified herein in the final rule.

                                EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Rowan supports the PFP's distinction between the interconnecting TSP and interconnecting DSP,
including separate definitions and the requirement that agreements identify each entity's
responsibilities, which is generally consistent with Rowan's prior recommendations.
Rowan supports the PFP's expansion of allowable site control methods to include an option to
purchase or lease at the intermediate agreement stage and a PSA at the interconnection agreement
stage, which is consistent with Rowan's prior advocacy for options and PSAs as acceptable forms
of site control at these stages.
Rowan supports the reduction ofthe financial security requirement from $100,000 per MW, which

development in Texas. While the reduction to $50,000 per MW moves the rule inthe right direction,

Rowan identifies a potential drafting issue in subsection (d)(1)(A), which references "contracted
peak demand" in the context ofthe intermediate agreement; Rowan recommends this be revised to
"requested peak demand," as the interconnection agreement establishing contracted peak demand
has not yet been executed at the intermediate agreement stage.
Rowan has significant concerns regarding the refundability provisions at both the intermediate
agreement and interconnection agreement stages, including the 80/20 forfeiture upon withdrawal
under subsections (g)(3)-(4), the non-refundable interconnection fee under subsection (f)(7), and
the five-year sustained operations requirement under subsection (i), and recommends that financial
security be fully refundable (less actual costs incurred) upon withdrawal or energization.
Rowan recommends that the Commission adopt a milestone-based refund schedule for refunds
related to energization, which would provide for 60% refund upon initial energization, 20% upon
achieving half of contracted peak demand, and the final 20% upon achieving full contracted peak
demand, rather than requiring five years of sustained operations. Rowan further recommends that
the dollar-per-MW financial security posted under subsection (d)(10) also be refundable upon
energization, and that the PFP address refunds where an interconnection study determines that the
interconnecting TSP cannot serve the large load customer's full requested peak demand or cannot
serve the requested peak demand on a commercially reasonable energization timeline, including
circumstances where the full MWs can be served only on a materially delayed schedule.
Rowan recommends that the PFP include a true-up process to ensure that financial security posted
under the intermediate agreement is properly credited toward interconnection agreement
obligations, and a refund process for intermediate agreement financial security that exceeds
interconnection agreement obligations.
Rowan identifies a potential drafting issue in subsection (f)(8)(B) regarding the sequencing of
financial obligations and recommends that the Commission clarify the acceptable forms of payment
for the interconnection fee under subsection (f)(7).
Rowan recommends that the PFP expressly permit a large load customer's tenant or other third
party with a written contract to post financial security and the interconnection fee directly to the
interconnecting TSP or DSP on behalf of the large load customer.
